setup: For three centuries before 1300, Europe had been warm — vineyards in England, Norse farmers growing cereals on Greenland, a population that doubled and built cathedrals, universities, and Crusades on the surplus. To feed all those people, every plowable acre got plowed, including marginal land that was too high, too cold, or too thin-soiled to ever have been farmed in a cooler world. That is the trap. Around 1300 the warmth runs out: summers cool by roughly 1°C, the growing season shortens, and the long cooling pulse historians call the Little Ice Age begins. A continent pushed right up against its agricultural limit suddenly loses the marginal yield it had grown to depend on. Nobody planned the farms around bad weather, because for three hundred years there hadn't been any. What is at stake here is whether a tightly stretched medieval Europe can absorb the first real shock of the new climate — and the answer, when three rainy summers hit in a row, is no.

bridge: Chapter 1 left Europe in a generation-long contraction. The Little Ice Age had cooled the summers, the Great Famine of 1315–1317 had killed roughly a tenth of northern Europe, and a cattle plague had wiped out the oxen that pulled the plows. By 1340 the high-medieval boom was clearly over — marginal farmland was being abandoned, the population had stopped growing, and a continent that had felt overcrowded in 1300 was quietly shrinking. It was a Europe already weakened, already short of slack, already in trouble. Then, from a direction nobody was watching, came the worst of it.
setup: In October 1347, Genoese galleys from the Black Sea port of Caffa put in at Sicilian Messina with their crews dying of black swellings. The disease is bubonic plague — Yersinia pestis, carried by rat fleas — and it has escaped its central Asian home along the trade routes the Mongols once kept safe. From Messina it moves at terrifying speed: Italy and Marseille within months, Paris by summer 1348, London by autumn, Scandinavia and Russia by 1350. There is no medical understanding of what causes it (germs are five centuries from discovery), no effective treatment, and no way to stop a disease that spreads through fleas and, in its lung form, through a cough. In four years it kills roughly a third of Europe. What is at stake is not one harvest or one kingdom but the entire high-medieval order — the labor system, the Church's authority, the relationship between lord and peasant, even who Europeans decide to blame. Everything in the chapters ahead happens in a Europe that has just been culled.

bridge: The first two chapters delivered the slow disasters — climate cooling, famine, and a plague that killed a third of the continent and kept coming back every decade or two. That is the backdrop against which kings kept fighting their wars. The Capetian dynasty that had ruled France since 987 had just run out of male heirs in 1328, and the French nobility chose a French nephew of the old king, Philip of Valois, over the English claimant. England, meanwhile, had held land in France since 1066, and the rich southwestern duchy of Aquitaine since 1152 — an arrangement that bred friction every generation. By 1337 the young English king Edward III decided the French throne was his by right, and went to war over it.
setup: What follows is the longest sustained war in European history — 116 years of fighting, with long pauses, conventionally called the Hundred Years War. The dynastic claim is mostly a pretext; the real engine is England's awkward landholding in France, control of the Flemish wool trade, and the deeper question of whether one nation can sit north of the Channel and another south of it. The war also breaks the rules of medieval combat. English longbows and dismounted men-at-arms shred the flower of French chivalry at Crécy and again at Poitiers and Agincourt; a century later, French cannon will return the favor at Castillon. In the middle of it all, with French royal authority at its lowest point in 435 years and the disinherited heir holed up south of the Loire, a teenage farmer's daughter from a frontier village walks in claiming the voices of saints have sent her to crown the king. What is at stake is which monarchy survives the war intact — and the answer turns on infantry, gunpowder, and one improbable nineteen-year-old.

bridge: While famine, plague, and the Hundred Years War were tearing at the body of Europe, the one institution that bound the whole continent together was tearing too. The Catholic Church of 1300 was the universal arbiter of Christian life — it crowned emperors, deposed kings, called Crusades, owned a third of the land, and provided the only ladder a peasant boy could climb. Every European we have met so far, from Dante to Joan of Arc, lived inside its sacraments and assumed its authority was self-evident and indivisible. This chapter is about how that assumption broke.
setup: It begins with a humiliation: in 1303, the French king's men physically arrest Pope Boniface VIII, who had just claimed that every human being must submit to the pope to be saved. The pope dies of the shock, and within a few years the papacy relocates to Avignon in southern France, where it stays for sixty-eight years under seven French popes — widely seen as French royal puppets running an extraction racket on the rest of Christendom. Worse follows. When the popes finally return to Rome, a disputed election in 1378 produces two popes at once, then three, each excommunicating the others, each telling ordinary Christians their salvation depends on backing the right man — with no way on earth to know which. The crisis forces a radical question into the open: who actually holds supreme power in the Church, the pope or a general council of bishops? What is at stake is whether the medieval Church can reform itself from within. The way that question gets answered will make the Reformation, a century later, almost unavoidable.

bridge: Chapter 4 ended with the Church reunited under one pope at Constance in 1417 but morally battered — three generations of Europeans had grown up watching rival popes excommunicate each other, and the institution had crushed every attempt to reform itself from within. The textbooks date the Reformation to Luther in 1517. But the doctrines, the anger, and even the armies came earlier. The same Council of Constance that healed the schism also burned a Czech preacher alive and dug up an English heretic's bones to scatter them — which tells you the Church already knew what it was up against.
setup: The men it was up against are John Wycliffe at Oxford and Jan Hus in Prague. Decades before Luther, Wycliffe articulates nearly the whole Protestant program — scripture above the pope, an attack on Church wealth and indulgences, a denial of priestly authority, and a Bible in English so anyone can read it. His ideas travel to Bohemia, where Hus preaches them in Czech to huge crowds. When the Church burns Hus at Constance in 1415 despite a written safe-conduct, Bohemia explodes into open revolt. What is at stake is whether a regional reformation, defended by the brilliant one-eyed general Jan Žižka and his armored war wagons, can break the Church a full century before Germany does. The Hussites will fight five papal Crusades to a standstill — and the only thing they lack is the technology that would, a lifetime later, let Luther's version go continent-wide.

bridge: The Black Death of Chapter 2 did something nobody legislated: by killing a third of the workforce, it handed the survivors enormous bargaining power. Wages doubled, serfs walked off the manor, and governments that tried to freeze wages back to pre-plague levels mostly failed. A peasantry that had been told for centuries to accept its place was now both materially stronger and newly assertive — and ground down, in France, by a Hundred Years War that left mercenary bands burning the very villages the nobility was supposed to protect. The combination was combustible.
setup: This chapter follows three of the largest popular uprisings of medieval Europe, all within a single generation. The Jacquerie of 1358 sees French peasants, sick of being pillaged after the disaster at Poitiers, burn noble manors across the countryside north of Paris. The Ciompi of 1378 sees Florentine wool-workers — laborers with no guild and no political voice — briefly seize the city government, the only direct rule by industrial workers in any major medieval city. The English Peasants' Revolt of 1381, lit by a hated flat poll tax and the egalitarian preaching of John Ball, marches on London, burns palaces, and beheads the Archbishop of Canterbury. All three are crushed within weeks; none win their stated demands. What is at stake is not really the immediate politics — it's whether the old assumption that the lower orders simply accept subordination can survive the post-plague world. It cannot, and the slow consequence is the quiet death of serfdom in the West.

bridge: So far this has been a story of catastrophe — climate, famine, plague, war, schism, revolt. But the same Italy that gave Europe the plague-bearing Genoese galleys, and the same century that watched a third of the continent die, was also producing something extraordinary. Petrarch, whom we met back in Chapter 1, had already started the hunt for lost classical manuscripts and the cult of individual genius. Now, in the patchwork of rich, competing Italian city-states, that current matures into the cultural moment later centuries would name the Renaissance — and it is less a sudden dawn than the late-medieval world entering its prime.
setup: The engine is fragmentation. Northern and central Italy hold some twenty independent city-states, with five big players — Venice, Genoa, militarized Milan, banking-and-textile Florence, and the kingdom of Naples — plus the Papal States, all competing for glory and all needing artists, architects, and scholars to provide it. Five courts mean five sets of patrons bidding against each other, and that competition funds a building boom, a portrait boom, and an intellectual boom that single-king monarchies elsewhere can't match. Florence's Medici bankers run the city without a crown and bankroll the whole project. Brunelleschi raises an impossible dome; Donatello and Masaccio reinvent sculpture and painting; in the north, the van Eycks perfect oil paint with microscopic realism. And in Mainz, a goldsmith named Gutenberg builds a machine that collapses the cost of a book tenfold. What is at stake is the foundation of the modern world's tools — and the press, especially, is the thing that will let the next century's revolutions go everywhere at once.

bridge: Across seven chapters the medieval order has been coming apart strand by strand: climate broke the farms, plague culled the people, the Hundred Years War killed chivalry, the schism shattered the Church's authority, Wycliffe and Hus rehearsed the Reformation, the peasants buried serfdom, and the Renaissance plus the printing press laid down the tools of a new age. This final chapter gathers the events that conventionally mark the curtain — most of them clustered in a single astonishing half-century, several of them in the single year 1492.
setup: In 1453 — the very year French cannon ended the Hundred Years War — Ottoman cannon batter down the thousand-year Theodosian Walls of Constantinople, and the Roman Empire, after more than two thousand years of institutional continuity, simply stops existing. England tears itself apart in the dynastic Wars of the Roses until a Welsh exile wins at Bosworth and founds the Tudor line. In 1492 Granada surrenders, ending 781 years of Reconquista; Spain expels its Jews; and a Genoese mariner with badly wrong geography stumbles onto a hemisphere nobody in the Old World knew existed. Portuguese ships round Africa and reach India by sea. What is at stake is nothing less than the shape of the next five centuries — but the chapter's real question is the slipperiest one in the book: when, if ever, did the Middle Ages actually end? There is no clean answer, only a transition stretching from roughly 1450 to 1550, and a sleeper who dozed off in 1300 and woke in 1500 would scarcely recognize the world.
